common_name: Black Lace Camellia (Dark Red Anemone-Form Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich, moist soil in partial shade; fall planting allows root establishment before the winter bloom season.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Black Lace is among the darkest-flowered camellia cultivars grown, its formal anemone-form blooms opening a deep, near-black red with a center boss of small petaloids in the same dark tone, giving each flower an unusually rich, velvety intensity compared to the brighter reds typical of most camellia cultivars. It blooms in mid to late winter on a slow-growing, dense, upright shrub with glossy dark-green foliage typical of Camellia japonica. Its dramatic dark color reads best against a light background — a pale wall, light mulch, or evergreen groundcover — where the depth of the flower color is not lost in shade. Prune, if needed, immediately after bloom in late winter or early spring, before next year's buds set.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich, moist soil in partial shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. A centuries-old Japanese cultivar discovered growing wild on an island off Nagasaki, Tama-no-Ura bears single to semi-double, rich red flowers crisply edged in white — a distinctive picotee pattern that has made it one of the most recognizable and widely propagated camellia cultivars in the world, grown far beyond its native Japan. It flowers over a long midseason window on a vigorous, upright shrub with the typical glossy, dark-green camellia foliage. Its bold red-and-white pattern reads clearly from a distance, making it an effective specimen or accent planting rather than a background shrub. Prune immediately after bloom in late winter or early spring, before the next season's flower buds set.

common_name: Dr. Tinsley Camellia (Blush Pink Semi-Double Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich, moist soil in partial shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Dr. Tinsley is a long-cultivated camellia prized for its soft, blush-pink, semi-double to peony-form flowers that shade from deeper pink at the petal base to nearly white at the edges, giving each bloom a gentle, watercolor-like gradation of color. It flowers over a long early-to-midseason window on a vigorous, upright, free-flowering shrub, and its dependable, prolific bloom has kept it a favorite among camellia collectors and Southern gardeners for generations. Its soft coloring makes it a versatile companion to more strongly colored camellia cultivars in a mixed planting. Prune immediately after bloom in late winter or early spring, before next year's flower buds set.

planting.note: Plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; blooms on old wood, so prune, if needed, immediately after flowering.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and remove the oldest flowered stems right after bloom to keep the compact shrub from becoming crowded at its base. Spilled Wine is a dwarf weigela roughly half the size of the species, producing dense, arching mounds of deep burgundy-purple foliage topped with a heavy flush of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers in late spring that draw hummingbirds reliably. Its small stature and consistently dark foliage make it a strong color-contrast shrub for the front of a mixed border or foundation planting where a full-size weigela would be too large. It is tough and adaptable, tolerating a range of soils once established, with minimal pruning needed given its naturally compact, well-behaved habit.

planting.note: Plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; deadhead spent flower clusters through summer to encourage continued rebloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and deadhead spent flower clusters through the summer to keep the rebloom cycle going. Unlike traditional weigela cultivars that flower only in a single spring flush on old wood, the Sonic Bloom series flowers on both old and new wood, producing a heavy spring display of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers followed by continued waves of bloom through summer into fall — dramatically extending the season of interest for a shrub usually valued for only a few spring weeks. Its hummingbird-attracting flowers and repeat bloom make it a strong choice where a longer season of color is wanted from a single shrub. Little pruning is required beyond removing dead or crossing branches, since rebloom on new wood makes timing far less critical than with old-wood-only weigela cultivars.

planting.note: Plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; variegation holds best with some direct sun but scorches in the hottest afternoon exposure.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from the harshest afternoon sun where summers are hottest. My Monet is among the smallest weigela cultivars available, forming a tight, mounded plant under a foot tall with green leaves crisply edged in white, often blushing pink along the margins in cooler weather, topped with a modest flush of small pink flowers in late spring. Its diminutive scale suits it to rock gardens, border edges, and container plantings where a full-size weigela would be far too large, and its variegated foliage provides season-long interest well beyond the brief bloom period. Prune only lightly if needed, and remove any solid-green reverted shoots as soon as they appear to keep the variegation stable.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; best foliage color develops in full sun.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear lightly after the main flush of bloom to refresh foliage color and encourage a tidy shape. Goldflame is one of the older and most widely planted foliage spirea cultivars, its new growth emerging a vivid coppery orange-red before maturing to bright gold through summer and finishing with orange-red fall tones, all set off by small clusters of pink flowers in early summer. Its compact size and long season of foliage color make it a workhorse for mixed borders and mass plantings where a low-maintenance shrub with more than a few weeks of interest is wanted. Extremely tough and adaptable, tolerating drought, poor soil, and urban conditions with minimal care once established.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear lightly after flowering to keep the mounded habit tidy and encourage fresh golden new growth. Gold Mound forms a low, dense, rounded mound of bright yellow-gold foliage that holds its color through the growing season better than many gold-leaved spirea cultivars, accented by flat clusters of small pink flowers in early summer. Its compact, tidy habit and reliable color make it a popular choice for low borders, foundation edges, and mass plantings needing consistent, low-maintenance color. Extremely tough and drought-tolerant once established, it tolerates poor soil and urban heat with minimal care.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear lightly after the main bloom flush to tidy the mound and encourage a modest rebloom. Little Princess is a compact, mounded spirea grown primarily for its abundant clusters of rose-pink flowers that blanket the blue-green foliage in early summer, rather than for foliage color as with the gold-leaved spirea cultivars. Its dense, tidy, low habit suits it to low hedges, foundation plantings, and mixed borders where a reliable flush of pink summer bloom is wanted on a plant that stays in bounds without heavy pruning. Extremely tough and drought-tolerant once established, tolerating poor soil and urban heat with minimal maintenance.

common_name: Double Play Spirea (Reblooming Compact Spirea Series)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; deadhead the first flush of flowers to encourage a stronger rebloom.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear off the first round of spent flowers to prompt a stronger summer rebloom. The Double Play series was bred by Proven Winners for extended flowering, combining colorful spring foliage — emerging in shades of orange, red, or burgundy depending on the specific selection — with an initial flush of pink to rose-red flowers in late spring and repeat bloom through summer into fall. Its compact, dense habit and long season of both foliage and flower interest make it a strong low-maintenance choice for foundation plantings and mixed borders. Extremely tough and drought-tolerant once established, tolerating poor soil and urban heat with minimal care.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; give Shasta ample width to display its horizontal branching habit without crowding.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing plenty of lateral room for the wide, tiered, horizontal branching this cultivar is known for. Bred by the U.S. National Arboretum, Shasta is among the most spectacular doublefile viburnum cultivars, its strongly horizontal, tiered branches lined in spring with rows of flat, lacecap-like flower clusters so dense the branches appear snow-covered, followed by red berries that ripen to black and draw songbirds in late summer. Its wider-than-tall habit makes it a strong specimen for open lawn areas or the edge of a woodland garden where its architectural branching pattern can be fully appreciated from a distance. Prune only lightly and selectively right after bloom, since heavy shearing destroys the natural tiered structure that is the plant's chief ornamental asset.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; for the heaviest berry set, plant at least two Brandywine (or a compatible seedling) shrubs together for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and plant a second, genetically distinct viburnum nudum nearby to ensure heavy fruit set, since this species needs a compatible cross-pollinator. Brandywine is a Southeastern native shrub selected for its extraordinary berry display: clusters of pink berries that ripen through shades of rose and blue to a deep, glossy blue-black, often showing several colors on the same cluster at once, held above glossy, dark-green, disease-resistant foliage that turns burgundy-red in fall. It tolerates consistently wet soil better than most flowering shrubs, making it a strong choice for rain gardens, pond edges, and low, poorly drained spots where many shrubs struggle. The berries are an excellent food source for songbirds, who typically strip them soon after they ripen.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring as new growth begins in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; growth is slow the first two seasons, so avoid overcrowding young plants.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and cut the whole clump back to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges. Aureola is the most widely grown Japanese forest grass cultivar, its cascading, arching, bamboo-like blades brightly striped in gold and green, lighting up dark corners of the shade garden with a luminous, almost glowing effect, especially where dappled light catches the foliage. The color intensifies in cooler weather and takes on pink-bronze tints in fall before going dormant for winter. Its slow-spreading, mounding habit works equally well as a woodland-edge groundcover, container specimen, or textural companion to hostas, ferns, and heuchera. Divide congested clumps in early spring every 4–5 years as growth increases.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; a few hours of morning sun deepens the gold stripe without scorching the foliage.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and comb out dead blades by hand each spring rather than shearing, since cutting the evergreen foliage back hard can leave the clump looking ragged for weeks. Evergold forms a neat, arching mound of narrow, grass-like leaves with a broad creamy-gold stripe down the center of each dark-green blade, brightening shaded borders and container plantings year-round in mild climates where the foliage stays evergreen through winter. Its compact, well-behaved habit and season-long color make it one of the most reliable variegated sedges for edging shaded paths and underplanting shrubs. Divide congested clumps in spring every 3–4 years to maintain vigor and clean color.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Ice Dance spreads by rhizome and can be used as a groundcover, so give it room or install an edging barrier where spread should be contained.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and comb out dead blades by hand each spring to keep the evergreen foliage looking tidy. Ice Dance produces glossy, dark-green, grass-like leaves crisply edged in white, spreading steadily by rhizome to form a dense, weed-suppressing patch more vigorously than clump-forming sedges like Evergold, making it useful as a shaded groundcover under trees or along shaded walkways where a spreading habit is an asset rather than a liability. Its crisp white-and-green variegation reads well even in deep shade where duller green groundcovers can look flat. Divide congested patches in spring as needed to control spread or propagate new plantings elsewhere.
